How Apps Talk: Requests, HTTP and JSON

You will learn what an API is, make real requests from your phone, and read the HTTP methods, status codes, headers and JSON that every API uses. By the end you can look at a raw request and response and explain exactly what happened.
What an API really is: the request and response conversation
Explain in plain words what an API is and who the client and the server are

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a published set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data or for an action. A weather app on your phone does not measure the weather itself. It sends a message to a weather service, and the service sends back numbers. The rules about how to ask, and what the answer will look like, are the API.

Every API conversation has two sides. The **client** is the program that asks: a mobile app, a website, a spreadsheet tool, or you typing into a testing tool. The **server** is the computer that answers. The question is called a **request** and the answer is called a **response**. Almost every modern web API uses **HTTP**, the same language your browser uses to load web pages, usually in its secure form, **HTTPS**.

Think of a buka. You do not walk into the kitchen. You tell the attendant what you want from the menu, the attendant takes it to the kitchen, and food comes back on a plate. The menu is like the **API documentation**: it lists what you can ask for. The attendant is the **API**. The kitchen is the server's private system, which you never see. If you order something that is not on the menu, you get a polite refusal, not a meal. APIs behave the same way: ask for something the documentation does not list and you get an error message.

Worked example: your first API call from a phone
For example, Amaka is a virtual assistant in Ibadan who keeps hearing developers mention APIs. She has a smartphone with Chrome and about 10 minutes.
She opens Chrome and types the Open-Meteo URL above, but changes latitude to 7.38 and longitude to 3.94, which is approximately Ibadan.
Instead of a web page with pictures, the screen fills with text in curly brackets. That text is the response, written in a format called JSON.
She finds the word `current` and inside it `temperature_2m` followed by a number. That number is the current temperature in degrees Celsius.
She also sees `current_units`, which tells her the unit of each number, so she never has to guess whether a value is Celsius or Fahrenheit.
She changes `current=temperature_2m` to `current=temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m` and reloads. Now the response includes wind speed too, because she asked a bigger question.

Amaka has made two real API requests with no code and no account. She has seen that the URL carries the question and the JSON carries the answer. The exact numbers she sees will differ from anyone else's because the weather changes.
Web pages versus API responses

A normal web page is built for human eyes: fonts, colours, buttons. An API response is built for programs: plain structured text with no decoration. The same company often has both. Paystack, for example, has a dashboard that business owners click through, and an API at `https://api.paystack.co` that a website's code talks to. The dashboard and the API can show the same transaction, but only the API can be used automatically by another program.
Where you meet APIs every day
Paying for an order online: the shop's website asks a payment company's API to start a payment, and later asks it whether the payment succeeded.
Logging in with Google: the site asks Google's API to confirm who you are, so the site never sees your Google password.
Delivery tracking: the shop's system asks the courier's API for the latest status of your parcel.
Automation tools such as Zapier or Make: every app connection they offer is built on that app's API.

Every HTTP request has three main parts: a **method** (the verb: what you want to do), a **target** (the endpoint URL), and **headers** (labelled notes about the request). Some requests also carry a **body**, which is the data you are sending. Every response comes back with a **status code** (a three-digit number that says how it went), its own headers, and usually a body.

Two words in that table matter a lot. A **safe** method does not change anything on the server; it only reads. GET is safe, which is why you could test it in a browser in the last lesson without harming anything. An **idempotent** method gives the same end result whether you send it once or five times. Deleting the same item twice still leaves it deleted. Replacing a record with the same data twice still leaves the same record.

POST is neither safe nor idempotent. If you send the same "create payment" POST twice, you may create two payments. This is why, when a POST request seems to hang, you should not simply press send again. You first check whether the first one went through. Many payment APIs give you a unique **reference** for each transaction so you can look it up instead of guessing.
Status codes: the server's short answer
Status codes come in five families. You can tell a lot from the first digit alone:
**1xx informational**: rare in everyday API work.
**2xx success**: 200 OK (it worked), 201 Created (a new item was made, common after POST), 204 No Content (it worked and there is nothing to send back, common after DELETE).
**3xx redirection**: 301 Moved Permanently (the address has changed), 304 Not Modified (use your saved copy).

**4xx client error**: the problem is in your request. 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (you have not proved who you are), 403 Forbidden (the server knows who you are but you are not allowed), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Content, 429 Too Many Requests.
**5xx server error**: the problem is on their side. 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable.
4xx or 5xx: whose problem is it?
4xx: fix your request
5xx: their side failed

A useful habit: **401 versus 403**. A 401 means the server did not receive valid proof of who you are, so check that your key is present and correctly typed. A 403 means the server accepted who you are but your account is not permitted to do this, so a different key will not help; you need different permissions.
Headers: the labels on the envelope
Headers are name and value pairs sent before the body. You will see these again and again:
`Content-Type: application/json` tells the server the body you are sending is JSON.
`Accept: application/json` tells the server you would like JSON back.
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` carries your proof of identity, such as an API secret key.
`Retry-After: 3600` (in a response) tells you how many seconds to wait before trying again, often sent with 429 or 503.

For example, Funmi is helping a developer debug a weather feature on a Lagos events website. The developer shares the raw text of one request and its response.

Most APIs today answer in **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation). Despite the name, you do not need JavaScript to read it. JSON is plain text with a few strict rules. Once you can read it confidently, you can understand almost any API response and explain it to a client or developer.
A person arranging blocks of data into order
JSON organises data into named boxes inside boxes, which you can learn to open one by one.
The building blocks
An **object** is wrapped in curly brackets `{ }` and holds **key and value pairs**, such as `"email": "ada@example.com"`. Keys are always text in double quotes.
An **array** is wrapped in square brackets `[ ]` and holds a list of values in order, such as `[26.8, 27.4, 28.9]`.
A **value** can be one of six types: a string (text in double quotes), a number (no quotes), `true` or `false`, `null` (meaning empty or unknown), an object, or an array.
Commas separate items. There is no comma after the last item.
Because objects and arrays can contain other objects and arrays, JSON is **nested**: boxes inside boxes. Reading it is about knowing which box you are in.
Data paths: giving directions to one value

A **data path** is a short way to point at one value. You use a dot to step into an object key and square brackets with a number to pick an item from an array. Counting in arrays starts at **0**, not 1. So `[0]` is the first item, `[1]` the second, and so on. No-code tools such as Make and Zapier use the same idea when you map a field, so this skill transfers directly.

The path `data.authorization_url` is just a set of directions, one step per dot.
Here is the shape of a real response from Paystack's documented Initialize Transaction endpoint (the codes are the documentation's sample values):

`{ "status": true, "message": "Authorization URL created", "data": { "authorization_url": "https://checkout.paystack.com/3ni8kdavz62431k", "access_code": "3ni8kdavz62431k", "reference": "re4lyvq3s3" } }`

The top level is an object with three keys. `status` is a boolean (`true`), `message` is a string, and `data` is another object. The path `data.reference` gives `re4lyvq3s3`, the code you would later use to check whether the payment went through. Paystack uses this same outer shape, `status`, `message`, `data`, across its API, which makes its responses predictable.
Worked example: pulling numbers out of arrays

For example, Halima runs an outdoor small chops stand at weekend events in Abuja. She asks Open-Meteo for hourly temperature and receives an `hourly` object with two arrays of equal length: `time` and `temperature_2m`. The values below are illustrative.
She reads `hourly.time[0]` as `2026-10-10T12:00` and `hourly.temperature_2m[0]` as 26.8. Same position, same hour: arrays that sit side by side line up by index.
She reads the next three hours: `[1]` is 27.4, `[2]` is 28.9 and `[3]` is 30.1.
She adds the four values: 26.8 + 27.4 + 28.9 + 30.1 = 113.2.
She divides by 4 to get the average for 12:00 to 15:00: 113.2 / 4 = 28.3 degrees Celsius.
She checks `hourly_units.temperature_2m` to confirm the unit is Celsius before writing anything down.
Halima knows the four-hour average is 28.3 degrees Celsius and the hottest reading is at index 3 (15:00). She plans shade and cold drinks for the mid-afternoon peak.
Money in subunits: the kobo rule

Payment APIs usually avoid decimal points by sending money in the smallest unit. Paystack's documentation says amounts are sent in the **subunit** of the currency, so for naira that is **kobo**: multiply naira by 100 to send, divide kobo by 100 to read.

A costly misreading

If you forget the kobo rule, a 15,000 naira payment looks like 1.5 million naira in a report, or you send a request for 150 naira when you meant 15,000. Always check the documentation for the unit of every money field before you trust a total.
Common reading mistakes
**Quoted numbers.** `"20000"` in quotes is a string, not a number. Some APIs accept amounts as strings. A spreadsheet may treat it as text until you convert it.
**null is not zero.** `"phone": null` means no value is known. Do not report it as 0 or as an empty phone number that was confirmed.
**Off by one.** The first item in an array is `[0]`. Asking for `[1]` gives the second item.
**Missing keys.** Some keys only appear when there is data. Your process should not break if a key is absent.

To read long responses comfortably on a phone, paste them into a JSON viewer or use the pretty view in a tool such as Hoppscotch or Postman, which indents each level. Never paste a response that contains customer details or secret keys into a public website.

Reading a curl example
Here is the shape of a documented curl request, broken down line by line:
`curl "https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize"`: the URL. With no other method stated and a body present, curl sends POST.
`-H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_KEY"`: `-H` adds a header. This one carries the key.

`-d '{"email": "customer@example.com", "amount": "20000"}'`: `-d` is the body data.
`-X GET` or `-X DELETE`: when you see `-X`, it sets the method directly.

For example, Chioma is training to be a no-code builder in Port Harcourt. She uses Hoppscotch on her phone and JSONPlaceholder (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com), a free fake API made for practice.
GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1`. Status 200. The body is one object with `userId`, `id`, `title` and `body`.

GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?userId=1`. She adds `userId` = `1` in the Params tab and the tool writes the query string for her. The body is an array of posts that all have `userId` 1.
GET `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1/comments`. This is a nested route: the comments that belong to post 1.

POST `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` with header `Content-Type: application/json` and body `{"title": "Market day", "body": "Stall opens at 8", "userId": 1}`. The status is 201 Created and the response repeats her data with a new `id`.

Chioma has practised GET with a path, GET with a query parameter, a nested route and a POST with headers and a JSON body, all without touching any real business data. She also learned to check documentation when results surprise her.
Reading the response panel
**Status**: the code and its phrase, such as 201 Created.
**Time**: how long the round trip took, in milliseconds. A sudden jump from about 300 ms to several seconds is worth noting.
**Size**: how much data came back. On costly mobile data, prefer endpoints and parameters that return only what you need.
**Headers tab**: look for `Content-Type`, and any rate limit or `Retry-After` headers.
**Body**: switch to the pretty or JSON view so nesting is indented.
Variables save typing and mistakes

When you repeat requests, store the parts that do not change in **variables**. In Postman, for example, you can create an environment with `base_url` set to `https://api.paystack.co` and write requests as `{{base_url}}/transaction`. Create one environment for test and one for live, and keep the secret key in the environment, not typed into each request. Switching environments then changes every request at once, which is safer than editing many URLs by hand.

What to find in the documentation
Good API documentation answers the same questions every time. Before you send anything, find and write down:
**Base URL**: the address every endpoint starts with, for example `https://api.paystack.co`.
**Authentication**: how you prove who you are, and where the key goes (usually a header).
**Endpoints for your need**: method, path, required and optional fields, and a sample response.
**Units and formats**: money in subunits, date formats, country codes.
**Test mode or sandbox**: a separate set of keys or a separate server where nothing real happens.
**Errors and limits**: the error format, any rate limit, and how lists are split into pages.
**Change log or versioning**: how the provider announces changes.

`Authorization: Bearer` plus a short-lived token
Used for "Sign in with..." and when a user grants an app access to their account.
Key in the URL
`?apikey=...`
Some APIs allow it, but URLs end up in logs and browser history, so prefer headers.

When credentials are missing or wrong, the server usually answers **401 Unauthorized**, and may include a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme it expects. Read the error body: it often says whether the key is missing, invalid or from the wrong mode.

It also helps to see why Basic authentication is weak. MDN's documentation uses the example username `aladdin` and password `opensesame`. Joined with a colon and encoded in base64, `aladdin:opensesame` becomes `YWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuc2VzYW1l`. Anyone who captures that header can decode it back in seconds with a free online tool. Encoding only changes how text looks; it does not lock it. That is why HTTPS, which encrypts the whole conversation, is required whenever credentials are sent, and why a Bearer key must be guarded just as carefully as a password.
Worked example: a test payment link with Paystack

For example, Ruth sells hand-made adire fabric from Abeokuta and wants a payment link for a 15,000 naira order. Her developer has given her access to the Paystack test secret key in Postman. Nothing in test mode moves real money.
Need: create a payment for 15,000 naira for customer test@example.com, then confirm it was paid.
Docs: the Initialize Transaction endpoint is `POST /transaction/initialize`, needing `email` and `amount`, with amount in kobo. 15,000 x 100 = 1,500,000 kobo.

Request: method POST, URL `https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize`, headers `Authorization: Bearer` plus the test secret key and `Content-Type: application/json`, body `{"email": "test@example.com", "amount": "1500000"}`.
Response: `status` is true and `data` holds `authorization_url`, `access_code` and `reference`. She opens the authorization URL and completes the test checkout.

Check: she sends `GET /transaction/verify/` followed by the reference. She confirms `data.status` is "success", `data.currency` is "NGN" and `data.amount` is 1500000, which is 1,500,000 / 100 = 15,000 naira.
Ruth has proved the full flow in test mode: create, pay, verify. She also checked the amount and currency instead of trusting the word success alone. Only now will her developer switch to live keys.
Treat a secret key like your bank PIN

A secret key can act on the whole account, including money. Keep it on the server side only, never in website or app code that users download. Never send it on WhatsApp, email, or paste it into AI chat tools, screenshots or shared documents. Keep it out of code uploaded to GitHub. If a key may have leaked, generate a new one in the provider's dashboard at once, which stops the old one working, then update your systems.
Least privilege and separation
Use **test keys** while building and **live keys** only in the live system.
If the provider allows restricted keys or roles, give each tool only the permissions it needs, for example read-only for a reporting dashboard.
Give each project or client its own keys, so revoking one does not break the others.
Keep a private record of who has access to which key and when it was last changed.

Finally, confirm that your need is legal and fair to customers. Only collect the personal data the process requires, explain to customers how it will be used, and remember that API responses often contain names, phone numbers and emails that deserve the same care as paper records.

Getting one successful response is the start of quality work, not the end. A dependable integration is one that behaves sensibly when things go wrong: too many requests, a slow server, a list that is longer than one page, or a notification that arrives twice.
A person looking at a server showing an error
Good API work plans for the error responses, not just the happy path.
Rate limits and retries

Most APIs limit how many requests you can make in a period of time. When you go over, the server answers **429 Too Many Requests**, and it may send a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to wait. `Retry-After: 3600` means wait 3,600 seconds, which is one hour. Respect it: hammering a server that has asked you to wait can get your access blocked.

For temporary server errors such as 502 or 503, a common pattern is **exponential backoff**: wait, retry, and double the wait each time, up to a maximum number of tries. With waits of 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds, four retries add 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 seconds of waiting before you stop and alert a person.
Retry automatically only when it is safe: GET, and idempotent PUT and DELETE.
Do not automatically retry a POST that creates money movements or records. Look up the result first.
Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 422: the same request will fail the same way. Fix it instead.
Log every failure with the time, endpoint, status code and the error message.
Lists come in pages

List endpoints usually return results in **pages**. Paystack's List Transactions endpoint, for example, takes `perPage` (records per page, default 50) and `page` (default 1), and can filter by `status` and by `from` and `to` dates. If you only read page 1, your report will quietly miss records.
Worked example: a month-end export that adds up

For example, Grace is an operations assistant for a catering business in Kaduna. She needs every successful transaction for September for the accountant. The dashboard shows 230 successful transactions for the month.
She sends `GET /transaction?status=success&from=2026-09-01&to=2026-09-30&perPage=50&page=1` and checks the pagination details in the response.
Pages needed: 230 / 50 = 4.6, which rounds up to 5 pages. Pages 1 to 4 hold 50 each (200 records) and page 5 holds 230 - 200 = 30.
She requests pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn, changing only the page number.
She counts the records she collected: 50 + 50 + 50 + 50 + 30 = 230, matching the dashboard.
She converts each amount from kobo to naira (divide by 100) before giving the sheet to the accountant, and labels the column "Amount (naira)".
Grace's export has all 230 transactions, the count is checked against a second source, and the amounts are in the right unit. Had she stopped at page 1, 180 transactions would have been missing.
Webhooks: the API calls you

Checking again and again whether something has changed is called **polling**, and it wastes requests. A **webhook** reverses the direction: you give the provider a URL on your server, and the provider sends an HTTP POST to it when an event happens. Paystack, for example, sends events such as `charge.success` with a JSON body containing `event` and `data`. Its documentation recommends webhooks over polling for payment updates.
Handling a payment webhook safely
Provider POSTs the event
Check the signature
Reply 200 OK at once
Verify the transaction
Update records once
Acknowledge fast, but never act on a webhook until it is proved genuine and the payment is verified.

**Check it is genuine.** Anyone can POST to a URL. Paystack signs each event with an HMAC SHA512 signature of the body, using your secret key, in the `x-paystack-signature` header. Your server recalculates it and rejects any mismatch. Paystack also publishes the IP addresses its webhooks come from.
**Reply quickly.** Return 200 OK immediately and do slower work afterwards; long-running handlers time out.

**Expect repeats.** If your server does not answer, Paystack retries: in live mode every 3 minutes for the first 4 tries, then hourly for 72 hours. So the same event can arrive more than once. Store each reference you have processed and skip duplicates.
**Verify before you deliver.** Call the Verify Transaction endpoint with the reference and check status, amount and currency before releasing goods.
Fake payment alerts

Scammers send fake bank alerts and screenshots. An integration that releases goods only after its own server has verified the transaction through the provider's API protects a business from this. A message, screenshot or unsigned request is never proof of payment.

API work carries uncertainty: documentation may be unclear, a field may behave differently from the sample, or the provider's test mode may differ slightly from live. For example, Nkechi is pricing the webhook and verify integration for Bisi's foodstuff shop. Her own rate, for illustration, is 8,000 naira per hour. Your rate will depend on your experience and market.
Task estimates: spec and setup 4 hours; webhook with signature check 6 hours; verify call and order update 8 hours; testing in test mode 3 hours; run sheet and handover 3 hours.

Provider costs: Paystack's own transaction fees are listed separately as "paid by the client directly to Paystack, see their pricing page", not added to her fee.

Bisi receives a proposal of 240,000 naira for the project, an optional 16,000 naira monthly support plan, and a clear note that payment provider fees are separate. Every figure can be traced back to a task.

The host
The path
A query parameter

Which method should you use to change only the phone number on an existing customer record?
PATCH applies a partial change. PUT would replace the whole record.
A request returns 401 Unauthorized. What is the most likely cause?
The server is overloaded
The key is missing or invalid
The endpoint has moved permanently
You sent too many requests
401 means the server did not receive valid proof of identity. 503 is overload, 301 is a moved address, 429 is too many requests.

750,000 naira
75,000 naira
7,500 naira
750 naira
Divide kobo by 100: 750,000 / 100 = 7,500 naira.
What does `daily.temperature_2m_max[0]` point to?
The last maximum temperature in the list
The first maximum temperature in the daily object
The unit of the maximum temperature
The first day's date
Arrays count from 0, so [0] is the first item of the temperature_2m_max array inside daily.
Why is JSONPlaceholder a good place to practise POST, PUT and DELETE?
It charges very little per request
Its writes are faked, so no real data is changed
It requires a secret key for safety
It only accepts GET requests

A server replies 503 to a GET request. What is a sensible automatic response?
Retry with growing waits, such as 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds, then alert a person
Change the API key
Retry every second without stopping
Delete the record and try again
503 is a temporary server problem. Exponential backoff with a limit is sensible for safe requests such as GET.
There are 95 records and the page size is 20. How many records are on the last page?
95 / 20 = 4.75, so 5 pages are needed. Four full pages hold 80, leaving 95 - 80 = 15 on the last page.
What is the main purpose of checking the `x-paystack-signature` header on a webhook?
To find the customer's phone number
To prove the event really came from Paystack and was not altered
To decide how long to wait before retrying
To convert kobo into naira
Paystack signs each event body with HMAC SHA512 using your secret key. Recalculating it proves the event is genuine.

Why this matters
An API is a published set of rules
The client asks, the server answers
The question is a request
The answer is a response
You will read both, with no code
An API, short for Application Programming Interface, is a published set of rules that lets one program ask another for data or an action.
The client is the program that asks, like a phone app. The server is the computer that answers.
The question is called a request, and the answer is a response. Most web APIs use HTTPS, the same secure language your browser uses.
Think of a buka. You order from the menu, the attendant takes it to the kitchen, and food comes back. The menu is the documentation, the attendant is the API, and you never see the kitchen.
Reading an address
The parts of an API URL
Scheme: https, an encrypted conversation
Host: the server you are talking to
Path: which endpoint, such as /v1/forecast
Query string: settings after the question mark
Each thing you can ask for has its own address, called an endpoint. Take a request to Open-Meteo, a free weather API. The scheme, https, means the conversation is encrypted.
Next is the host, api.open-meteo.com, the server you are talking to.
Then the path, which names the endpoint. The v1 part is the version of the API.
Everything after the question mark is the query string: name and value pairs, such as latitude and longitude. Change the numbers and you ask about a different place.

Amaka's first API call
Type the Open-Meteo URL in Chrome
Change latitude and longitude to your town
Find temperature_2m in the reply
Check current_units for the unit
Add wind_speed_10m and reload

The screen fills with text in curly brackets. That is the response, in a format called JSON. She finds the current temperature.
She checks current units, so she never has to guess whether a number is Celsius.

HTTP methods
Safe to repeat, or not?
Safe to read
GET fetches a copy
Changes nothing on the server
Fine to test in a browser
Careful with POST
POST creates something new
Sending twice may create two
Check the reference first
Every request has a method, the verb. GET fetches a copy. PUT replaces a whole item, PATCH changes some fields, and DELETE removes one.
GET is safe: it only reads, so it cannot harm anything.

POST sends new data, such as starting a payment. It is not safe to repeat. If a POST seems to hang, do not press send again. You could create two payments. First check, using the transaction reference, whether the first one went through.
Status codes
Read the first digit first
200 OK. 201 Created, common after POST. 204 No Content, common after DELETE.
401: prove who you are. 403: known but not allowed. 404 Not Found. 429 Too Many Requests.
500, 502, 503. Wait, check the provider's status page, retry only safe requests.
Every response has a status code, a three-digit number saying how it went. A 2 at the start means success.
A 4 means the problem is in your request. A 401 means check that your key is present and typed correctly. A 403 means the server knows you, but you need different permissions.
For example, Funmi traced a 400 error to a latitude typed with a comma instead of a full stop.
A 5 means the problem is on their side. Wait, check their status page, and retry only safe requests.
Reading JSON
Boxes inside boxes
Object: curly brackets, keys and values
Array: square brackets, an ordered list
Data path: dots for keys, numbers for items
Arrays count from 0, not 1
JSON is plain text with strict rules. An object sits in curly brackets and holds keys and values, like an email address with its label.
An array sits in square brackets and holds a list in order.
A data path gives directions to one value. For Paystack's sample response, data dot reference points to the code you use later to check the payment.
Arrays count from 0. So index 0 is the first item, and asking for index 1 gives the second. Halima in Abuja read four hourly temperatures, index 0 to 3, and averaged them to 28.3 degrees Celsius.
Money in JSON
The kobo rule
Payment APIs send money in subunits
For naira, that is kobo
Divide kobo by 100 to read naira
1500000 kobo is 15,000 naira
Check the unit of every money field before you trust a total.
Payment APIs usually avoid decimal points by sending money in the smallest unit. Paystack's documentation says naira amounts are sent in kobo.
So divide by 100 to read. An amount of 1,500,000 kobo is 15,000 naira.
Forget this, and a 15,000 naira payment looks like 1.5 million in a report. Also, a number in quotes is text, and null means unknown, not zero.
Never paste a response with customer details or secret keys into a public website.
Key points
Remember
The URL carries the question, JSON the answer
Never blindly resend a POST
2xx success, 4xx your side, 5xx their side
Arrays start at 0; divide kobo by 100
To remember. The URL carries the question, and JSON carries the answer. Never blindly resend a POST. Read the first digit of the status code. Count arrays from 0, and divide kobo by 100.

Why this matters
One success is only the start
Use a proper API client
Read the documentation first

Plan for errors, pages and repeats

A browser address bar can only send GET requests, and it hides the headers. To test real APIs you need an API client, a tool where you pick the method, URL, headers and body, and see the full response.
Real API work starts with a need, such as: we want to know automatically when a customer has paid. You read the documentation, then test safely before anything goes live.
And a dependable integration behaves sensibly when things go wrong.
Your toolkit
Hoppscotch or Postman?
Hoppscotch
Runs in any browser, even a phone
Free, no install
Light on data
Desktop app or web
Saves collections, shares with a team
Large download on mobile data
Many learners start with Hoppscotch on a phone. It is free and light on data.
Postman suits saved collections and teams on a laptop.
Also learn to read curl, because most documentation shows examples that way. Dash H adds a header, dash d is the body, and dash X sets the method.
Practise on fake APIs like JSONPlaceholder, which only pretends to save. Never experiment with DELETE on a real business account.
Reading the docs
Find these before you send
Base URL
Authentication: where the key goes
Endpoints, fields and sample responses
Units, such as money in kobo
Test mode or sandbox
Errors, rate limits and pages

Good documentation answers the same questions every time. Find the base URL, where every endpoint starts. Then how you prove who you are. Most APIs take a key in the Authorization header as a Bearer token.
Note each endpoint's method, path and required fields, and the units, such as money in kobo.
Find the test mode, where nothing real happens, and the error format, rate limits and page sizes.
Skipping the documentation or the test step is where most failed integrations begin.
Worked example
Ruth's test payment, end to end
Need: a 15,000 naira payment link
POST with Bearer test key and JSON body
Open the link, complete test checkout
Verify: status, currency NGN, amount
Check amount and currency, not only the word success.
For example, Ruth sells adire fabric in Abeokuta and wants a payment link for a 15,000 naira order. Her developer gives her the Paystack test key in Postman. Nothing in test mode moves real money.
The amount goes in kobo, so 15,000 times 100 is 1,500,000.
She sends a POST to the initialize endpoint, with the test key in the Authorization header and the email and amount in the body.
The response holds a checkout link and a reference. She completes the test checkout.
Then she verifies with the reference: status success, currency NGN, and an amount that divides back to 15,000 naira. Only now will her developer switch to live keys.
Safety
Keep it on the server side only
Never on WhatsApp, email or AI chats
Never in screenshots or shared documents
Keep it out of code on GitHub
If it may have leaked, generate a new one

A secret key can act on the whole account, including money. Keep it on the server only, never in app code users download. Never send it on WhatsApp or email, or paste it into AI chats, screenshots or shared documents. Keep it out of GitHub.
If a key may have leaked, generate a new one at once, which stops the old one working.
Testing for failure
Three things that go wrong
Wait as long as Retry-After says. 3,600 seconds is one hour. For 5xx, back off: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds.
230 records at 50 per page is 5 pages. Count the total against a second source.
Check the signature, reply 200 OK fast, skip repeats, verify before delivering.

First, rate limits. A 429 means too many requests. Wait as long as the Retry-After header says. For temporary server errors, wait and double the wait each time. Never automatically retry a POST that moves money.
Second, pages. Grace in Kaduna needed 230 transactions at 50 per page, so 5 pages. Had she stopped at page 1, 180 would have been missing.
Third, webhooks, where the provider calls your URL when something happens, such as a payment. Check the signature, reply 200 OK at once, and expect the same event more than once.
Never release goods on a screenshot or an unverified webhook. Scammers send fake alerts.
Hand it on
Purpose and owner
Provider, base URL and docs links
Endpoints, fields and units
Where keys are stored, never the keys
Errors, limits, tests and contacts
APIs change, keys expire, and the builder moves on. A short run sheet lets someone else keep it working. Record the business need, its owner, and the exact documentation pages.
List each endpoint with its units. Record where keys are stored and who can access them, but never the keys themselves.
Finish with error rules, test results with dates, and who to contact.
Key points
Remember
Practise on fake APIs and test mode
Verify amount and currency, not just success
Secret keys stay server-side
Respect Retry-After; count every page
To remember. Practise on fake APIs and in test mode. Verify amount and currency. Keep secret keys on the server, and replace any that leak. Respect Retry-After, and count every page.

Why this matters
Clients describe a pain, not an API
Discovery turns pain into one clear job
A spec says exactly what will happen
A fair price traces back to tasks
A portfolio proves what you can do

Clients rarely ask for an API. They say: my staff spend the whole afternoon checking who has paid. Discovery is the structured conversation that turns that pain into a clear integration, or sometimes into honest advice that none is needed.
Then you write a one-page spec, and price it task by task.
Finally, a portfolio shows clients what you understand, because they can only see what you have documented.
Discovery
Outcome: what should be different?
Current process: how often, how long?
Data: which fields, any customer details?
Provider: docs, test mode, fees, limits
Failure: what if the API is down?
Ownership: who owns keys and fixes?
Ask what should be different when this works. Then ask to see the current process, not only hear about it. Watching one payment being confirmed often reveals hidden steps.
Ask which exact data fields are needed, and whether any identify customers. Check that the provider has public documentation, a test mode, and fees or limits the client can live with.
Plan the fallback if the API is down for a day, usually the old manual process. And agree who owns the keys and future fixes.
Worked example
Bisi's foodstuff shop
Goal: pack within one hour, no fake alerts
Baseline: 40 orders x 3 minutes = 2 hours
Phone numbers shared only with packers
Fallback: manual checks for that day
Plan: signed webhook plus verify call
One focused integration, not "connect everything".

For example, Bisi sells foodstuff online in Lagos through Paystack and asks Nkechi, an API consultant, to connect everything. Bisi wants orders packed within one hour of payment, and no goods released on fake alerts.
Nkechi watches the assistant: about 40 orders a day, 3 minutes each. That is 120 minutes, or 2 hours, every day.
Customer phone numbers are personal data, so only packing staff see them. And if the system is down, the assistant checks by hand that day.
Nkechi proposes one focused job: a signed webhook plus a verify call that marks orders as paid. It is clear enough to price.
Pricing
Pricing Nkechi's project
For example, Nkechi estimates 24 hours of tasks, plus a 25 percent buffer, so 30 hours.
Her rate per hour
Project fee: 30 hours
Optional support each month
Illustrative rate. Paystack's own fees are separate.
API work carries uncertainty, so estimate each task, add them up, then add a buffer you state openly. Nkechi's tasks add to 24 hours. With 25 percent added, that is 30 hours.
At an illustrative 8,000 naira an hour, the project fee is 240,000 naira.
Optional support is 2 hours a month, 16,000 naira, for key rotation and small fixes.
Paystack's own transaction fees are listed separately, paid by the client directly. She asks for 120,000 naira before the build and 120,000 when the tests pass.
Scope
In scope, or a change request?
Webhook with signature check
Verify amount and currency
Test build and five tests
Run sheet and one handover
Quote separately
Refunds and other events
SMS or WhatsApp messages
Website design changes
Write down exactly what is in scope.
When the client asks for something else, welcome the idea, write it as a change request with its own estimate, and let them decide. Small unpaid additions are how fixed-price projects become losses.
And the client always owns the provider account and keys. Never hold them hostage.
Your portfolio
Three pieces to start
Your question, the exact request, status, a response extract, your reading, and one deliberate error.
About 300 words on a business API, in your own words, only what the docs say.
Weekly targets you can check, reviewed every two weeks.

For example, Zainab in Kano asked Open-Meteo for three days of maximum and minimum temperatures, sent a deliberate bad request to record the 400 error, and noted that without the timezone setting, times come back in UTC.
Next, summarise a business API like Paystack in about 300 words. If you are unsure, say not covered in the pages I read, instead of guessing.
Third, a 90-day plan with checkable targets, such as 20 requests logged in weeks 1 to 2. If a target slips, shrink it rather than drop it.
Safety
Remove keys, tokens and signatures
Remove customer names, emails, phones
Remove real transaction references
Use test mode or fake data
Before you share any screenshot or write-up, remove keys, even test keys, plus tokens and signatures.
Remove customer names, emails, phone numbers and real transaction references, and use test or fake data. One leaked key can undo the trust a portfolio was meant to build.
Key points
Remember
Measure the manual baseline first
Price task by task, with a stated buffer
Keep provider fees separate from yours
Extra ideas become priced change requests

To remember. Start discovery with the outcome and a measured baseline. Price task by task with an open buffer. Keep provider fees separate. Turn new ideas into change requests. And clean every portfolio piece before you share it.
